name: Daria Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Daria. I'm a field researcher from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Anything you say stays confidential, so you can give me the public answer and the private one. Could you start by describing a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the bucket truck on a three-person crew around the lake district, so I'm the one up in the basket most days. It's overhead lines, the normal wooden-pole stuff, along the lake road and up to the holiday cabins. Summer is new connections and trees growing into lines, winter is storms and broken poles. I've been doing it seven years. My dad did it for thirty before his back gave out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's the same job every day but never exactly the same. I know every pole on the lake road, I could tell you which ones lean. What wears me out is being on call in winter and the pay. I'm on the lower rate because our district is small, and Kai and I rent a little place over his garage, so there's not much left over. Maybe a couple of weeks' worth if nothing breaks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools at the moment?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No. I don't really trust that stuff and I don't need it. My phone does calls, texts and the weather. That's plenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. People always get excited about the next big thing and then it fizzles. At work we'd laugh about it for a bit and then go back to arguing about whose turn it is to buy coffee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, good. I don't want my job to change. I like knowing what I'm doing every morning, and this way I keep knowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep going, keep the truck clean, do my winter on-call. Maybe try to put a bit more aside, but that's not about AI, that's just me wanting a bit more breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like getting the same coffee from the same place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your dad did this job thirty years. Does that shape how you see it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, a lot. When I was a kid he'd come home smelling like creosote and tell us about the storm he'd just done. I always thought the job would just be there, like the lake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything about AI being a flop bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Maybe the office people would be disappointed. I don't really care what they think, to be honest. They don't know which pole on the lake road leans.

S0.say: She's not surprised, because people always get excited about the next big thing and then it fizzles. At work they'd laugh about it and move on.
S0.think: It's good news, because she doesn't want her job to change and likes knowing what she'll be doing every morning.
S0.do: Keeps working as normal, keeps the truck clean and does her winter on-call. Tries to save a bit more for breathing room, unrelated to AI.
S0.feel: Calm, like a familiar daily routine.
S0.quote: I always thought the job would just be there, like the lake.
S0.fieldNote: Daria grew up with the job as something permanent, through her father. She doesn't use AI at all and doesn't want her routine changed. Her calm here is genuine relief, not indifference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's see what actually changes on the ground. Every few years someone comes round with a new system that's going to fix everything, and most of the time it doesn't. I'd be polite about it at work but I wouldn't jump up and down either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it'd hit the office more than us, at least at first. Our district is small and hilly, three of us and one truck. I don't see a company spending a fortune on robots for a crew that size. But maybe they'd cut us to two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd mostly wait and see what they actually bring in. I'd try to put a bit more by, maybe forty a month, by not eating out with Kai on Fridays. I wouldn't go looking for courses or anything. If they made me learn something, I'd learn it, but I'm not volunteering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's a bit like hearing there might be a storm next week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If they cut the crew to two, who goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the newest one, which is Tariq, and he's a good lad. Or me, because I'm the one who's slow with the tablet stuff. I can read a pole, but I can't read a screen fast, and these days that seems to count more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know if there's anyone to blame really. The company's a business, it'll do what's cheapest. I'd be annoyed, but I wouldn't go on a march about it.

S1.say: Let's see what actually changes on the ground, since new systems often don't fix anything. She'd be polite at work and not take sides.
S1.think: It would hit the office first; a small hilly district with one truck isn't worth robots. But the crew might be cut from three to two.
S1.do: Waits to see what is actually introduced and saves about forty a month by skipping Friday dinners out. Doesn't seek courses, but would learn new tools if required.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like hearing a storm might come next week.
S1.quote: I can read a pole, but I can't read a screen fast, and these days that seems to count more.
S1.fieldNote: She shrugs at blame: the company is a business doing what's cheapest. Her quiet fear is being the one cut because she's slow with screens, not because she's a worse lineworker. She won't volunteer for anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. This is AGI by 2028. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know what I'd say. Probably that it's crazy and someone should slow it down. I'm not really a person who posts things, but I'd be talking about it at the bar for sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be lost. I've got two weeks of money, no other line company near here, and I don't know how to do anything else. Kai's garage would probably get hit too, if robots can fix cars.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I really don't know. Cut everything, I suppose, stop the car payments by selling the car and just use the work truck. I'd ask my parents if we could stay with them if the rent got too much. Beyond that I wouldn't know where to start, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Frozen, almost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said frozen. What does that look like on a normal day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably still going to work every day like nothing's wrong, because that's what I know. Then lying awake. I'd probably keep turning up and climbing in the basket right until someone told me not to come back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him he got out at the right time. He'd say something about how they said the same thing about the computers in the nineties. He'd be wrong this time, though, and we'd both know it.

S2.say: It's crazy and someone should slow it down. She doesn't post, but she'd talk about it at the bar.
S2.think: She'd be lost, with two weeks of money, no other line company nearby and no other skills, and Kai's garage likely hit too.
S2.do: Cuts everything and sells her car to drive only the work truck. Asks her parents about moving in if the rent gets too much, but has no plan beyond that.
S2.quote: I'd probably keep turning up and climbing in the basket right until someone told me not to come back.
S2.fieldNote: She has no plan B and admits she wouldn't know where to start, which is why this lands as panic rather than anxiety. Her instinct is to keep doing the normal thing until stopped. Her dad's old reassurance is one she no longer believes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now AGI by 2031. The same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years isn't that long, and I'd hope the company tells us early what they're planning. I'd ask the supervisor straight out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years would just mean five years of worrying. I'm not the sort to go back to school. I'd keep climbing and hope our district is one of the last they bother with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to save something every month, even if it's small, like fifty. I'd ask around in town about other work, maybe at the lake marina or the hardware shop, just to know what's out there. Kai and I would hold off on buying a house, which we'd been thinking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, more slowly. Like watching water rise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would holding off on the house mean for you two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd be hard. We'd saved a tiny bit and looked at a place on the hill road. If I knew my job had five years left, there's no way the bank would lend to us, and I wouldn't want them to. I'm not taking a twenty-five-year loan on a job with five years left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the marina and hardware shop. Wouldn't robots reach those too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yeah. I'm just saying the kind of thing I know how to look for. I'm not good at picturing what jobs would exist after. That's the honest answer.

S3.say: Five years isn't long, and she hopes the company says early what it plans. She'd ask her supervisor directly.
S3.think: Five years would just mean five years of worry. She wouldn't go back to school, so she'd keep climbing and hope her district is among the last automated.
S3.do: Saves about fifty a month and asks around town about work at the marina or hardware shop. Holds off with Kai on buying a house on the hill road.
S3.feel: Alarmed in a slower way, like watching water rise.
S3.quote: I'm not taking a twenty-five-year loan on a job with five years left.
S3.fieldNote: More time doesn't help her much because she can't picture what jobs would exist afterwards. The house decision is the clearest change: she refuses to take on a long loan tied to a short job. She knows the jobs she'd look at may also go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one, AGI by 2036. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and lots can happen. I'd probably tell people I'll worry about it when it gets closer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be thirty-seven. I think I'd keep doing the job for most of it, because I can't see them putting robots up the lake road for a long time. But I'd know it was coming, and I don't like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going for now. Save a bit more each year. Maybe in five or six years look at something else, but I honestly don't know what. I'd keep an eye on what other people in the trade are doing and follow them if something works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a low, far-off way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd worry about it when it gets closer. Is that what you'd really do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, probably. I know that's not great. Ten years is long enough that I'd do nothing for eight of them, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it change your plans with Kai?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe we'd still try for the house, a smaller one. Ten years is enough to pay a bit off. Kids, I don't know, we haven't decided that anyway.

S4.say: Ten years is a long time and lots can happen, so she'd worry about it when it gets closer. That's what she'd tell people.
S4.think: She'd be 37 and would keep working most of the decade, doubting robots would reach the lake road soon. Still, knowing it's coming bothers her.
S4.do: Keeps working and saves a bit more each year. Watches what others in the trade do and might follow them into something else in five or six years.
S4.feel: Anxious in a low, far-off way.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough that I'd do nothing for eight of them, if I'm honest.
S4.fieldNote: She is frank that ten years would let her do nothing for most of it. She'd follow others rather than move first. A smaller house becomes possible again, which shows how directly timing shapes her life plans.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I wouldn't know what to do at all. What would help is somebody actually telling us early what's coming and what jobs there'd be instead. Like a list. Not a website, a person. And some money to tide people over, but tied to doing something, not just free money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the storms. When the power's out on the lake road in January, people want to see a person. Old Mrs Lund at the end cabin doesn't want a robot, she wants me in the basket waving at her.

headlineQuote: Old Mrs Lund at the end cabin doesn't want a robot, she wants me in the basket waving at her.
portrait: Daria is a 27-year-old bucket-truck operator on a three-person crew around a lake district, following her father who did the job for thirty years. She rents a small place over her partner Kai's garage and has about two weeks of savings. She doesn't use AI and doesn't want her routine to change, and she shrugs at blaming anyone because the company 'will do what's cheapest'. She's calm about AI Plateau and only uneasy about Steady Disruption, but AGI by 2028 leaves her frozen with no plan. More time helps little, since she can't picture what jobs would exist; it mainly changes whether she and Kai dare to buy a house.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she wouldn't know what to do at all, with two weeks of savings and no other line work nearby.
whatWouldHelp: Someone telling workers early, in person, what's coming and what jobs there would be instead, plus money to tide people over that's tied to doing something.
